noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand the role of enzymes as biological catalysts in metabolic reactions

primer.text: Enzymes are the protein machines that keep metabolism running fast enough for life. This note explains why they are called biological catalysts, how the active site recognises its substrate, and how the enzyme-substrate complex forms and releases its products — the mechanism behind almost every reaction you will meet in this course.

lessons.title: Biological catalysts and the active-site mechanism
lessons.opening: An enzyme is a protein made inside living cells that speeds up a chemical reaction without being changed itself. Without them, a single meal would take weeks to digest; with them it takes hours. Each enzyme recognises one substrate because its active site is complementary in shape, forming a complex that breaks apart to release products.
keyPoints: Enzymes — proteins made inside living cells — speed reactions up as biological catalysts without being changed or used up.
They are made in living cells, which is what the word biological adds.
Each enzyme's active site is complementary in shape to its particular substrate.
Substrate binding forms the enzyme-substrate complex; products then leave and the enzyme works again.

low.restatement: Enzymes are protein catalysts from living cells: the substrate fits the active site, the reaction happens, products leave, and the enzyme is ready to work again.
low.analogy: An enzyme works like a vending machine for one exact coin: the right coin (substrate) drops in, the snack (product) drops out, and the machine resets for the next coin.
low.examPointer: The phrase 'without being changed or used up' is the mark-earning clause in catalyst definitions — never omit it.

medium.restatement: Catalysis lowers the barrier so metabolic reactions run at life-compatible speeds; specificity comes from shape complementarity, and the complex step explains why products no longer fit the site.
medium.analogy: A good catalyst is a matchmaker that ends each event single again — it introduces substrate partners, steps back, and repeats.
medium.examPointer: Link the three-step mechanism (random movement, collision, product release) to the collision idea when explaining how rate changes with temperature.

check.stem: Which statement defines an enzyme correctly?

options.text: A protein made in living cells that speeds up reactions without being changed
options.explanation: All three defining clauses appear: protein, living origin, unchanged catalyst.

options.text: A carbohydrate that stores energy in cells
A lipid that forms cell membranes
options.explanation: Membrane lipids are structural, not catalytic.

options.text: A protein that is consumed by each reaction it speeds up

check.stem: Why is each enzyme specific to one substrate?

options.text: Because substrates are all identical
options.explanation: Substrates differ; sites match particular shapes.

options.text: Its active site has a shape complementary to that substrate
options.explanation: Shape complementarity is the stated cause of specificity.

options.text: Because the substrate is larger than the enzyme
Because enzymes carry the substrate's DNA

check.stem: What happens to the enzyme after the products leave its active site?

options.text: It keeps the products locked in place
options.explanation: Products leave because they no longer fit.

options.text: It changes into the product itself
options.explanation: The enzyme never becomes the product.

options.text: It is unchanged and free to bind another substrate molecule
It is destroyed and must be remade

check.stem: Which sequence describes the mechanism of enzyme action in order?

options.text: Products released first, then the substrate binds
Substrate moulds the enzyme into a new enzyme
The enzyme digests the substrate's DNA
Random movement, collision forming the complex, reaction, products released
options.explanation: This is the note's three-step account.

check.stem: Digestion without enzymes would take roughly two to three weeks per meal; with enzymes about how long?

options.text: Around four hours
options.explanation: The note contrasts weeks with hours — about four.

options.text: Around four minutes
Around four weeks
Around four days
options.explanation: The note names hours, not days.

check.stem: State the name of the region where a substrate binds an enzyme.
What name is given to the combined structure formed when a substrate sits in an enzyme's active site?
Explain why the products of the reaction no longer fit the active site they were made in.
check.modelAnswer: The active site is shaped to the substrate, not to the products; once the reaction has rearranged the substrate into product molecules their shapes differ, so they no longer match the site and are released, leaving the enzyme ready for the next substrate.

check.stem: A detergent advert promises stain removal at low wash temperatures. Using the catalyst idea, state what the added enzymes do to the stain molecules and why they survive the wash.
check.modelAnswer: The enzymes catalyse the breakdown of stain molecules into smaller, soluble pieces at speed; they survive because catalysts are not consumed by the reactions they speed up.

glossary.definition: A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being changed or used up itself.
The region of an enzyme whose complementary shape receives its specific substrate.
The temporary combined structure formed while a substrate sits in an enzyme's active site.
Any of the chemical reactions that together make up an organism's metabolism.
